title: Does oil speculation increase gas prices?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether oil speculation drives up gasoline prices. They open with the Obama administration's energy security policy (reducing oil imports by a third over a decade, pressure on oil companies to develop leased acreage) and high gas prices (around $3.60 a gallon national average, $4.11 peak in 2008). They weigh supply factors such as Libya's civil war, Saudi Arabia's production increase, and peak oil, then explain futures contracts, going long and short, and how derivatives trading can create an unstable market. They cover the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the 2000 Enron loophole, the Intercontinental Exchange's move to American terminals, the conflicting 2008 International Energy Agency and follow-up reports, the failed Consumer First Energy Act, and Frederick Kaufman's Harper's article on the food bubble. The episode closes with listener mail from Melanie about sperm donor conception and a half-sibling reunion, which she asked the hosts to cover.

segments.title: Opening banter and White House energy call
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the show and discuss a call with a senior White House official about Obama's energy security policy and goal of cutting oil imports by a third over ten years.

segments.title: Oil leases and gas price context
segments.summary: Discussion of oil companies holding leases on about seventy-nine million acres while about nineteen million are in production, and the Obama administration's push for them to produce. The hosts cite a $3.60 national average gas price and recall the 2008 spike to $4.11.

segments.title: Gas price history and supply factors
segments.summary: The hosts compare gas prices from 2004 to 2008 and discuss the rise in crude oil prices over that period. They then review instability in oil-producing regions, including Libya's civil war, Carl Levin's comments on instability, Hugo Chavez's heating oil donations through CITGO, and Saudi Arabia's offer to add production.

segments.title: Peak oil and supply versus demand
segments.summary: The hosts discuss peak oil, the view that supply should keep prices low under Adam Smith's economics, and why oil is treated as a vital commodity. They say the question of why prices keep rising is where speculation comes in.

segments.title: How oil futures work
segments.summary: Josh explains futures contracts using a buyer and seller example, the concepts of going long and going short, and the difference between taking delivery and trading the contract. He notes that futures are derivatives and that most trading happens before expiration.

segments.title: Speculation and the argument that it inflates prices
segments.summary: The hosts explain how derivatives speculation could create an unstable market and push the spot price up through hoarding and rumor. They cite an investigation finding Vitol held eleven percent of NYMEX oil futures contracts and mention Goldman Sachs and Citigroup. They note that low interest rates push money from investment banks into commodities.

segments.title: CFTC, Enron loophole, and ICE
segments.summary: The hosts cover the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's role in policing speculation and how its oversight weakened. They describe the 2000 Enron loophole for over-the-counter trading and the Intercontinental Exchange, which traded European oil futures from Atlanta and later set up American terminals in New York.

segments.title: Debate over speculation's effect and the Consumer First Act
segments.summary: The hosts describe a July 2008 International Energy Agency report that found speculation had little effect, followed by a September report that found correlations. They mention the Consumer First Energy Act, which would have extended CFTC oversight to foreign markets and died on the Senate floor, and mention Frederick Kaufman's Harper's article on the food bubble.

segments.title: Listener mail: sperm donor family story
segments.summary: Lizzie reads an email from Melanie, a college student in South Korea, about learning her real father through a sperm donor after growing up without information about him, and finding a half-brother. She asks for an episode on sperm and egg donation. The hosts note the request and close the mail segment.
